p3: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?
Do you think older people are more stubborn than younger people?
What kinds of things can persuade people to change their minds?
Is it a sign of weakness when a politician changes their position?
How has social media affected the way people form their opinions?
p3samples: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?

I think it's largely a question of pride. Once someone has said something publicly, backing down can feel like losing face, especially in cultures where reputation matters a lot. On top of that, our opinions are often tied to our identity, so if you challenge someone's view on, say, politics or religion, they may feel that you're attacking them personally rather than just their argument. That makes people defensive rather than open-minded.
Is it a sign of weakness when a politician changes their position?

Not necessarily. If new evidence emerges, I'd actually respect a politician more for adjusting their policy than for sticking to a plan that clearly isn't working. The problem is when the change seems to be driven purely by opinion polls rather than by principle. Voters can usually tell the difference, so I'd say what matters is whether the leader explains their reasoning honestly.

p2.card: Describe a skill you learned online.
bullets: where and how you learned it
how long it took you to learn
p2.explain: and explain how useful this skill has been for you.
p2.sample:
The skill I want to describe is basic video editing, which I taught myself entirely online about two years ago. At the time I was helping a friend promote her small bakery, and she wanted short clips for social media, but neither of us could afford to pay a professional.

So I started searching on YouTube for beginner tutorials. I found one channel in particular that was brilliant, because the presenter broke everything down into ten-minute lessons, such as how to cut clips, add music and adjust the colour. I'd watch a lesson in the evening, then immediately try it out on my own footage. Later I signed up for a cheap online course that came with practice files and a community forum, which was really handy whenever I got stuck.

In terms of how long it took, I'd say I could produce something decent after about a month, but it took me nearly half a year before I felt genuinely confident. The hardest part was learning the keyboard shortcuts and getting the timing right, so that the cuts matched the rhythm of the music.

As for how useful it's been, honestly it's opened quite a few doors. My friend's bakery got noticeably more customers after we started posting regularly, and since then I've edited videos for a couple of family weddings and even a small project at work. More importantly, it showed me that I'm capable of learning something technical on my own, which has given me the confidence to take on other online courses.
vocab: chia nhỏ mọi thứ ra cho dễ hiểu
p3: What are the advantages of learning online compared with learning in a classroom?
Which skills are difficult to learn online?
Why do many people start online courses but never finish them?
Should employers accept online qualifications in the same way as traditional degrees?
How might technology change education in the future?
p3samples: Why do many people start online courses but never finish them?

The main reason, I think, is the lack of accountability. In a physical class there's a teacher who notices if you're absent and classmates you don't want to fall behind. Online, nobody really cares whether you log in, so when work or family gets busy, the course is the first thing to go. Also, many courses are free or very cheap, and people tend not to value things they haven't invested much money in.
Which skills are difficult to learn online?

Anything that relies heavily on physical feedback is tricky. For example, learning to swim or to play a musical instrument properly really requires someone to watch you and correct your posture or technique in real time. Interpersonal skills are another area, like negotiating or managing a team, because you need to practise with real people and deal with unpredictable reactions, which a video simply can't replicate.

p2.card: Describe a building you find interesting.
p2.explain: and explain why you find it interesting.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about the old central post office in Ho Chi Minh City, which is right in the heart of District 1, just across the square from the cathedral. It was built by the French at the end of the nineteenth century, and it's still one of the most striking buildings in the city.

From the outside, it has a pale yellow facade with tall arched windows and a large clock above the entrance. But what really impresses me is the interior. When you walk in, you find yourself in an enormous hall with a high, curved ceiling supported by green iron columns, and there are two huge hand-painted maps on the walls showing the region as it was over a hundred years ago. There's also a portrait of Ho Chi Minh at the far end, so it's a mixture of colonial and modern history in one space.

The interesting thing is that it isn't just a museum. It's still a working post office, so you'll see local people sending parcels and paying bills right next to tourists taking photos. There are a few stalls selling postcards and souvenirs as well.

I find it fascinating for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it shows how a building can stay useful for well over a century instead of being knocked down and replaced. And secondly, it reminds me how complicated our history is. Every time I go there, usually when friends visit from abroad, I notice some little detail I'd missed before, like the patterns on the floor tiles.
vocab: one of the most striking buildings
một trong những toà nhà nổi bật nhất
bưu điện vẫn đang hoạt động
bị đập bỏ và xây lại
p3: Should governments spend money preserving old buildings?
What makes a building attractive in your opinion?
Do you think modern cities look too similar to each other?
Who should have the final say in the design of public buildings?
How will buildings change in the future because of climate change?
p3samples: Should governments spend money preserving old buildings?

I believe they should, at least for buildings with real historical or architectural value. They give a city its character and help people feel connected to the past, and they're often a big draw for tourists, so the investment can pay for itself. That said, it isn't realistic to protect everything. Governments need clear criteria, otherwise preservation can block much-needed housing or infrastructure.
Do you think modern cities look too similar to each other?

To some extent, yes. If you look at the business districts of many Asian capitals, they're full of almost identical glass towers, shopping malls and international chains. I suppose it's because developers use the same global firms and the same cost-effective designs. It's a bit of a shame, because when you travel you want to feel you're somewhere distinctive, so I think architects should draw more on local materials and traditions.

p2.card: Describe a time when you helped a stranger.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about helping this person.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe something that happened last rainy season, on my way home from work. It was around six in the evening, and there had been a sudden downpour, so the street near my flat was partly flooded.

As I was walking past a bus stop, I noticed an elderly man standing next to a motorbike that had obviously broken down. He was soaked, and he looked quite distressed because he kept trying to start the engine and nothing was happening. Lots of people were rushing past, probably because they just wanted to get out of the rain.

I went over and asked if he needed a hand. It turned out the water had got into the engine, and he lived about three kilometres away, which was too far to push the bike. So first I lent him my raincoat, then I helped him wheel the motorbike to a small repair shop just round the corner. The mechanic said it would take about an hour, so I bought him a hot drink from a nearby cafe and we sat and chatted while we waited. He told me he was a retired teacher and that he'd been visiting his daughter in hospital.

To be honest, it was only a small thing, but I felt really good afterwards. I think what struck me most was how grateful he was, since he kept thanking me for weeks whenever he saw me in the neighbourhood. It also made me realise how easy it is to ignore people when we're in a hurry, so now I try to pay more attention to what's going on around me.
vocab: cơn mưa như trút bất chợt
điều làm tôi ấn tượng nhất
p3: Why are some people reluctant to help strangers?
Are people in cities less helpful than people in the countryside?
Should children be taught to help others at school?
What kinds of volunteer work are common in your country?
Do you think technology makes people more or less willing to help each other?
p3samples: Why are some people reluctant to help strangers?

One reason is fear, I suppose. People worry that the situation might be a scam, or that they could get into trouble if something goes wrong. Another factor is what psychologists call the bystander effect: when lots of people are around, everyone assumes someone else will step in, so nobody does. And of course, in busy cities people are often rushing and simply don't notice that someone needs help.
Are people in cities less helpful than people in the countryside?

I'd say people in the countryside tend to be more helpful, but mainly because they know each other. In a village, if your neighbour's roof is damaged, everyone turns up to help since they've got long-term relationships. In a city you're surrounded by strangers, so the sense of obligation is weaker. That doesn't mean city people are less kind, it's just that the social ties are looser.

p2.card: Describe an app on your phone that you use often.
p2.explain: and explain why you find it useful.
p2.sample:
The app I use most often, apart from messaging apps, is a budgeting app that tracks my spending. I started using it about eighteen months ago, after I realised that I was always running out of money a few days before payday and had no idea where it was going.

It's quite simple really. Every time I spend money, I enter the amount and choose a category, like food, transport or entertainment. If I pay by card, it can actually link to my bank account and record the transaction automatically, which saves a lot of time. At the end of each week it shows me a pie chart of my spending, and I can set a monthly limit for each category. When I get close to the limit, it sends me a little warning, which is surprisingly effective.

I mainly use it in the evenings, just for a couple of minutes to check everything's been recorded properly. I also use it when I'm planning bigger purchases, for example last year I used it to save up for a new laptop.

The reason I find it so useful is that it's completely changed my attitude towards money. Before, I'd buy coffee or snacks without thinking, but when I saw that I was spending almost a fifth of my salary on takeaway drinks, I was genuinely shocked. Now I'm much more careful, and I've managed to build up a small emergency fund. So for me, it isn't just an app, it's helped me develop a much healthier habit.
vocab: dành dụm một khoản quỹ dự phòng
một thói quen lành mạnh hơn
p3: Why are some apps so popular with young people?
Do you think people spend too much time on their phones?
Should parents limit the amount of time children spend on apps?
How have apps changed the way people shop?
Is it safe to store personal information on apps?
p3samples: Do you think people spend too much time on their phones?

Generally speaking, yes. I see families at restaurants where everyone is scrolling instead of talking, and that worries me a little. Many apps are deliberately designed to be addictive, with endless feeds and notifications that pull you back in. Having said that, a lot of screen time is productive, like working, studying or keeping in touch with relatives abroad, so I think the issue is how we use phones rather than just the number of hours.
Is it safe to store personal information on apps?

It depends on the app and the company behind it. Big banks usually invest heavily in security, so I'm fairly comfortable using their apps. But there are plenty of free apps that collect far more data than they need, like your contacts or location, and sometimes sell it to advertisers. So I'd say people should read the permissions carefully and avoid giving access unless it's genuinely necessary.

p2.card: Describe a piece of good advice you received.
p2.explain: and explain how this advice has helped you.
p2.sample:
The best piece of advice I've ever been given came from my first manager, when I'd just started working at a small marketing company. I was about twenty-two and very eager to impress, so I said yes to absolutely every task anyone gave me.

After about three months, I was completely exhausted. I was staying late almost every night, and the quality of my work was actually getting worse because I was rushing everything. One afternoon my manager called me into her office. I assumed I was in trouble, but instead she asked me how many projects I was working on. When I told her, she just smiled and said, "If everything is a priority, then nothing is a priority." She explained that being reliable doesn't mean doing everything; it means doing the important things well and being honest when you can't take on more.

She then showed me a really practical method. Every Monday morning, I should list all my tasks and pick the three that would make the biggest difference that week. Anything else, I could either postpone, hand over to someone, or politely decline.

At first it felt uncomfortable to say no to colleagues, but the results were obvious within a few weeks. I was leaving on time, my work was more accurate, and ironically people started trusting me with more interesting projects. Even now, years later, I still do that Monday list. I think the advice was valuable not just for work but for life in general, because it taught me that protecting my time and energy isn't selfish, it's sensible.
vocab: háo hức muốn gây ấn tượng
gặp rắc rối, bị khiển trách
từ chối một cách lịch sự
p3: Who do young people usually go to for advice in your country?
Is advice from older people still relevant today?
Why do some people ignore good advice?
Should people pay for professional advice, such as from a financial adviser?
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?
p3samples: Is advice from older people still relevant today?

Some of it is and some of it isn't. When it comes to technology or the job market, older people's advice can be a bit outdated, since things have changed so quickly. But advice about relationships, patience or handling difficult times is pretty timeless. My grandparents lived through very hard periods, so when they talk about resilience, I think it's worth listening to even if the world looks different now.
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?

I think it depends on the kind of problem. For technical issues, like a legal question or a health concern, you obviously need an expert, because friends might give well-meaning but inaccurate advice. For personal decisions, though, friends are often better, because they know your personality and circumstances. Ideally you'd combine both: get the facts from a professional and then talk it through with people who know you well.

p2.card: Describe a noisy place you have been to.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the noise.
p2.sample:
One of the noisiest places I've ever been to is a wholesale market in my city, which I visited early one morning last year. A friend of mine runs a small restaurant, and she invited me to come along while she bought fresh vegetables and seafood for the week.

We got there at around four in the morning, and I was amazed by how lively it was. There were hundreds of trucks unloading crates, motorbikes weaving in and out with enormous loads, and traders shouting prices at the top of their voices. On top of that, there was the constant sound of ice being crushed for the fish stalls, and loudspeakers playing announcements. It was so loud that my friend and I had to stand very close just to hear each other.

My job was mostly to follow her around and help carry the bags. I watched her bargain with the sellers, which was quite an art in itself, because she would pretend to walk away, and then they'd call her back with a better price. We also stopped at a tiny stall for a bowl of noodles before heading back.

As for how I felt about the noise, it was overwhelming at first, and I actually got a slight headache after about an hour. But after a while I started to appreciate it, because the noise was really a sign of how hard-working everyone was. It gave the place a real energy that you don't feel in a quiet supermarket. Still, I was very relieved to get home and enjoy a bit of peace and quiet afterwards.
vocab: chợ đầu mối, chợ bán sỉ
at the top of their voices
choáng ngợp, quá sức chịu đựng
p3: What are the main sources of noise in cities today?
How does noise pollution affect people's health?
Should there be stricter laws about noise in residential areas?
Why do some people prefer noisy places to quiet ones?
How can city planners make urban areas quieter?
p3samples: How does noise pollution affect people's health?

The most obvious effect is on sleep. If you live next to a busy road or a construction site, it's hard to get proper rest, and over time that can lead to stress, poor concentration and even heart problems, according to some studies I've read. Children in noisy schools also seem to struggle more with reading, because they find it harder to focus. So it's a more serious issue than many people realise.
How can city planners make urban areas quieter?

There are quite a few practical measures. Planting trees and building green barriers along major roads can absorb a surprising amount of sound. Planners can also keep industrial zones away from housing and encourage electric buses, which are far quieter than diesel ones. Another idea is to create car-free streets in the centre, which not only reduces noise but also makes the area more pleasant for pedestrians.

p2.card: Describe a family tradition that is important to you.
p2.explain: and explain why this tradition is important to you.
p2.sample:
A tradition that means a lot to me is the way my family marks my great-grandmother's death anniversary every year. In Vietnam, we call this a gio, and for my family it's almost as important as the Lunar New Year.

It takes place on the same day of the lunar calendar every year, usually some time in autumn. Wherever we are, all the relatives try to come back to my grandparents' house in the countryside, so it's one of the few occasions when three or even four generations are under one roof.

The preparation starts the day before. The women in the family, and these days some of the men as well, spend hours cooking traditional dishes, like sticky rice, boiled chicken and spring rolls. The children help to clean the house and arrange flowers and fruit on the ancestral altar. On the day itself, my grandfather lights incense and says a few words to remember her, then everyone takes turns to bow in front of the altar. After that, we all sit down together for a huge meal, which usually goes on for hours with a lot of laughing and storytelling.

The reason it's so important to me is that it keeps the family connected. I never met my great-grandmother, but through the stories my relatives share each year, I feel as if I know her. It also reminds me where I come from. My cousins and I are scattered across different cities now, so without this tradition, I think we would gradually drift apart.
vocab: sống rải rác ở nhiều nơi
p3: Why are traditions important for society?
Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
How have family traditions changed in your country?
Should traditional festivals become public holidays?
Can globalisation threaten local traditions?
p3samples: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?

I wouldn't say they're less interested, but they often take part in a different way. For instance, young people might not spend days cooking traditional food, but they'll happily share photos of the festival online or join a modern version of it. Busy work schedules and living far from home also make it harder for them. So the interest is there, it's just being expressed in a more flexible form.
Can globalisation threaten local traditions?

It certainly can. When global brands and foreign holidays like Halloween or Valentine's Day become heavily commercialised, they can overshadow local festivals, especially among children. On the other hand, globalisation can also help traditions survive, because tourists become interested in them and communities realise their cultural value. The key, I think, is for schools and families to keep explaining the meaning behind local customs, not just the activities.

p2.card: Describe a plan you made that you had to cancel.
bullets: why you had to cancel it
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about cancelling it.
p2.sample:
I'm going to talk about a camping trip that my university friends and I had planned for months but ended up cancelling at the last minute. It was supposed to be a three-day trip to a national park in the Central Highlands, and there were six of us involved.

We'd organised everything really carefully. One friend had booked a campsite and a local guide, someone else had borrowed tents and sleeping bags, and I was in charge of transport, so I'd reserved seats on an overnight coach. We even had a group chat where we shared a detailed packing list and a menu for each day. Since we'd all started full-time jobs, it was quite difficult to find dates that suited everyone, so we were really looking forward to it.

Unfortunately, about two days before we were due to leave, a big tropical storm was forecast for the region. At first we hoped it would change direction, but then the park authorities announced that the trails would be closed for safety reasons. So, very reluctantly, we decided to call it off. Luckily, the coach company gave us a partial refund, though we lost the deposit for the guide.

I was genuinely disappointed, because I'd been counting down the days. But I also knew it was the right decision, as heavy rain in the mountains can cause landslides. To make up for it, we spent that weekend together in the city instead, cooking the camping food on a friend's balcony, which turned out to be surprisingly fun. And we've already rescheduled the trip for next spring.
p3: Why do people often fail to stick to their plans?
Is it better to plan everything in advance or to be spontaneous?
How do people in your country usually plan holidays?
What kinds of events are most often cancelled because of the weather?
Do you think people today plan their lives further ahead than in the past?
p3samples: Is it better to plan everything in advance or to be spontaneous?

I think a balance is best. For important things like travel during a busy holiday season, planning ahead is essential, otherwise flights get expensive or fully booked. But if you plan every hour of a trip, you lose the chance to discover things by accident, which is often the most memorable part. So I usually book the essentials and leave some free time to see what happens.
Do you think people today plan their lives further ahead than in the past?

In some ways yes, and in others no. People now plan their careers and finances more carefully, for example saving for retirement or choosing a degree based on job prospects. But personal milestones like getting married or buying a home are often postponed and less predictable than they were for my parents' generation, partly because the economy feels less stable. So life planning has become more detailed but also more uncertain.

p2.card: Describe a sport you would like to try in the future.
bullets: what you would need to do it
p2.explain: and explain why you would like to try it.
p2.sample:
A sport I'd really love to try is rock climbing, and in particular outdoor climbing on real cliffs rather than just indoor walls.

I first became interested in it a couple of years ago when I watched a documentary about a climber who scaled an enormous granite wall in the United States without any ropes. To be honest, that looked absolutely terrifying, and it's definitely not something I'd attempt. But it made me curious, so I started following a few climbing channels online, and I learned that there are some great climbing spots in Vietnam too, especially on the limestone cliffs around Ha Long Bay and in the north.

As for what I'd need, obviously I'd have to start with proper training, probably at an indoor climbing gym, to learn the basic techniques and how to use the safety equipment. You need special shoes, a harness, a helmet and a chalk bag to keep your hands dry. And for outdoor climbing, it's essential to go with an experienced instructor who knows how to set up the ropes properly. I'd also need to work on my upper body strength, because at the moment I can barely do a single pull-up.

The main reason I want to try it is that it seems to combine physical fitness with problem-solving. Climbers talk about each route as a kind of puzzle, where you have to plan your next move carefully. I think that would be a great way to switch off from work. Also, I've always been slightly afraid of heights, so I'd like to challenge myself and hopefully overcome that fear.
vocab: thư giãn, tạm quên công việc
p3: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?
Should dangerous sports be banned or more strictly controlled?
What can schools do to encourage children to take up sport?
Why are some sports more popular than others in your country?
Do professional athletes earn too much money?
p3samples: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?

For many people, it's about the adrenaline rush. Doing something risky makes them feel intensely alive, which is hard to get from everyday life sitting at a desk. There's also a strong sense of achievement when you complete something that seemed impossible, like a difficult climb or a big wave. And I think social media plays a role as well, because dramatic photos and videos from these sports attract a lot of attention.
Should dangerous sports be banned or more strictly controlled?

I don't think banning them is the answer, because adults should be free to take risks with their own safety. However, I do support stricter regulation of the businesses that offer them. Instructors should be properly certified, equipment should be checked regularly and customers should be told clearly about the risks. That way people can still enjoy these activities, but the number of avoidable accidents would go down.

p2.card: Describe a time when you were late for something important.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about being late.
p2.sample:
I'd like to describe the morning I was late for a job interview, which still makes me cringe when I think about it. It was about three years ago, and the interview was for a position at a logistics company that I was really keen to join.

I'd actually planned everything quite carefully. The interview was at nine, and I set off at eight, which should have given me plenty of time. The problem was that, just as I joined the main road, I discovered there had been an accident on a bridge, and the traffic came to a complete standstill. I was stuck there for nearly forty minutes, and to make matters worse, my phone battery was almost dead because I'd forgotten to charge it the night before.

I managed to send a quick message to the recruiter, apologising and explaining the situation, before my phone switched off. In the end, I arrived about twenty-five minutes late, out of breath and sweating. Fortunately, the manager was very understanding. She had seen the news about the accident, so she simply moved my interview to the end of the morning, and I got the chance to calm down first.

I felt awful at the time, mostly embarrassed, because first impressions really matter in interviews. But in a strange way, it turned out well, since I got the job, and later my manager told me she was impressed that I'd let them know in advance rather than just turning up late without warning. Since then, I always leave much earlier than necessary, and I never go to anything important without a fully charged phone.
vocab: khiến tôi thấy ngượng chín người
hụt hơi, thở không ra hơi
p3: Is punctuality important in your culture?
Why are some people always late?
Should companies allow employees to choose their own working hours?
How has technology changed the way people manage their time?
Do you think people today have less free time than in the past?
p3samples: Why are some people always late?

I think it's often because they're overly optimistic about how long things take. They assume the journey will take twenty minutes in perfect conditions, without allowing for traffic or delays. Some people also try to squeeze in one more task before leaving, like answering an email. And for a few, it might be a personality thing, they simply don't feel the same pressure about time that others do.
How has technology changed the way people manage their time?

In some ways it's made it much easier. We've got calendar apps that remind us about appointments and maps that predict exactly how long a journey will take. But technology has also become one of the biggest distractions. People intend to check one message and end up scrolling for half an hour. So I'd say the tools are better than ever, but self-discipline has become even more important.

p2.card: Describe a friend who is good at solving problems.
bullets: what kind of problems they solve
p2.explain: and explain why you think this person is good at solving problems.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about my friend Minh, who I've known since we were in the same class at high school. We actually got to know each other because we were put in the same group for a science project, and while the rest of us were arguing about what to do, he quietly drew a plan and divided up the tasks. I was impressed even then.

These days, he works as an engineer for a water company, so solving problems is basically his job. But what I really admire is how he deals with everyday problems for the people around him. For example, when my laptop crashed the night before an important deadline, he spent hours helping me recover my files. Another time, when our friend's small shop was struggling, he sat down with her and worked out a much simpler way to keep track of her stock.

I think there are a few reasons why he's so good at it. First of all, he stays remarkably calm. When most people panic, he just asks questions to understand what's actually going wrong. Secondly, he breaks big problems into smaller steps, so they seem much more manageable. And thirdly, he isn't afraid to admit when he doesn't know something. He'll happily look it up or ask someone who knows more, instead of pretending.

Honestly, I've learned a lot from him. Whenever I'm faced with something difficult now, I try to ask myself what Minh would do, which usually means slowing down, thinking logically and not letting my emotions take over.
p3: Is problem-solving a skill that can be taught?
What kinds of problems do young people face today?
Do people rely too much on the internet to solve their problems?
Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?
Which jobs require the strongest problem-solving skills?
p3samples: Is problem-solving a skill that can be taught?

I believe it can, at least to a large extent. Some people are naturally more logical, but things like breaking a problem into parts, testing different solutions and learning from mistakes are techniques anyone can practise. Schools could do more of this through project-based learning, where students tackle real issues instead of memorising answers. That kind of experience builds confidence as well as skills.
Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?

It really depends on the problem. For something simple or very personal, working alone is quicker and you don't need to compromise. But for complex issues, a team is usually better because people bring different knowledge and perspectives, and someone might spot a flaw you'd missed. The danger with teams is that discussions can drag on, so you need someone to keep things focused.

p2.card: Describe an old object that your family has kept for a long time.
p2.explain: and explain why your family has kept it for so long.
p2.sample:
The object I'm going to describe is an old sewing machine that has been in my family for over fifty years. It's one of those heavy black machines with gold patterns painted on the side, and it's operated by a foot pedal rather than electricity.

It originally belonged to my grandmother. She bought it second-hand in the early nineteen-seventies with money she'd saved for almost two years, and it basically became her livelihood. She used it to make clothes for neighbours and to do repairs, and with the money she earned, she was able to pay for my father and his brothers to go to school. My dad often says that machine put them through education.

These days, it's kept in the corner of my parents' living room, covered with a cloth to protect it from dust. Surprisingly, it still works perfectly. My mother uses it now and then to shorten trousers or fix curtains, and when I was a child, my grandmother taught me how to sew a straight line on it, which I found quite difficult because you have to coordinate your hands and feet.

I think the reason we've kept it for so long is that it represents my grandmother's determination and the sacrifices she made for the family. Every time I look at it, I'm reminded of how hard life was for her generation and how much we owe them. My parents have already said they'd like me to keep it one day, and I'll definitely look after it, because to me, it's far more valuable than any modern appliance.
vocab: những hy sinh bà đã làm
chúng ta mang ơn họ nhiều như thế nào
p3: Why do people keep old objects?
Do you think people today throw things away too easily?
What kinds of objects are often passed down in families in your country?
Should museums display everyday objects as well as valuable ones?
Are people becoming less attached to physical possessions because of digital technology?
p3samples: Do you think people today throw things away too easily?

Definitely. Many products are now made to be cheap rather than durable, so when something breaks, it's often cheaper to buy a new one than to repair it. Fashion is a good example, because people buy clothes, wear them a few times and then discard them. This creates a huge amount of waste. I think governments should support repair shops and require manufacturers to make spare parts available for longer.
Are people becoming less attached to physical possessions because of digital technology?

In some areas, yes. Hardly anyone keeps photo albums or CD collections now, since everything is stored on phones or in the cloud. But I'm not sure people are less attached overall. If anything, physical objects like handwritten letters or old cameras have become more special precisely because they're rare. So technology may have reduced the quantity of things we keep, but increased the sentimental value of the ones we do.

p2.card: Describe a podcast or radio programme that you enjoy.
bullets: what it is called and what it is about
how you found out about it
p2.explain: and explain why you enjoy it.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about a history podcast I've been listening to for about a year. It's presented by two British historians, and each episode focuses on one event or person from the past, anything from ancient Egypt to the space race. The episodes are usually about forty-five minutes long, and a new one comes out every week.

I found out about it quite by chance. A colleague mentioned it during a lunch break when we were chatting about a film set in the Second World War, and she said there was a brilliant series of episodes about the same period. I downloaded one that evening and I was hooked almost immediately.

I mostly listen to it while I'm commuting, since my journey to work takes about thirty minutes each way. I also put it on when I'm doing housework, like washing up or ironing, because it makes boring jobs go much faster.

There are several reasons I enjoy it so much. First, the presenters have a great chemistry. They tease each other and make jokes, so even when the topic is serious, it never feels like a dry lecture. Second, they're very good at telling history as a story, with lots of vivid details about ordinary people's lives, which helps me remember it. And finally, it's been surprisingly good for my English. Because I'm listening to natural conversation rather than scripted dialogue, I've picked up loads of useful expressions and become much more comfortable with British accents, which I used to find quite challenging.
vocab: làm việc nhàm chán trôi qua nhanh hơn
học lỏm được cách diễn đạt
p3: Why have podcasts become so popular?
Do you think radio will disappear in the future?
Is listening to something a good way to learn?
Should the government fund public broadcasting?
How reliable is the information people hear on podcasts?
p3samples: Why have podcasts become so popular?

Mainly because they fit easily into busy lives. You can listen while you're driving, exercising or cooking, so it doesn't feel like you're giving up extra time. There's also an incredible variety, so whatever your interest, from gardening to economics, there's probably a show about it. And I think people like the informal, conversational style, which feels more personal and authentic than traditional broadcasting.
How reliable is the information people hear on podcasts?

It varies enormously. Some podcasts are produced by established news organisations or experts who check their facts carefully. But since anyone can start a podcast with just a microphone, there are also many shows where hosts present personal opinions as facts, sometimes on topics like health. So listeners need to think critically, check who's behind the show and compare what they hear with other sources.

p2.card: Describe a time when you had to wait for a long time.
bullets: what you did while you were waiting
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the wait.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe a time I had to wait for almost nine hours at an airport. It was a couple of years ago, when I was flying back from Singapore after a short work trip.

My flight was supposed to leave in the early afternoon, but when I got to the gate, there was an announcement that it had been delayed because of a technical problem with the plane. At first they said it would be about two hours, so I wasn't too worried. But then the delay kept getting longer and longer, and in the end, they had to bring in a replacement aircraft from another city, so we didn't take off until nearly midnight.

As for what I did while waiting, I tried to make the best of it. I had my laptop, so I spent a couple of hours finishing a report I'd been putting off. After that, I wandered around the terminal, which, luckily, is one of the best airports in the world for this kind of situation. There's an indoor garden, a butterfly enclosure and even a small cinema, so I explored all of that. The airline also gave us meal vouchers, so I had a nice dinner, and I ended up chatting with a couple from Australia who were on the same flight.

To be honest, I was quite frustrated at first, mostly because nobody was giving us clear information. But by the end I felt fairly relaxed. I realised there was nothing I could do to change the situation, so getting angry would only have made it worse.
vocab: tận dụng tối đa tình huống
p3: In what situations do people usually have to wait in your country?
Are people today less patient than in the past?
How can businesses reduce waiting times for customers?
Is patience an important quality for children to learn?
Why are some people willing to queue for hours for new products?
p3samples: Are people today less patient than in the past?

I think so, generally. We've become used to instant results: food delivered in twenty minutes, films streamed immediately and messages answered within seconds. So when something takes longer, like a slow website or a long queue, people get irritated very quickly. My grandparents, by contrast, were used to waiting weeks for a letter, so they seem much calmer about delays than my generation.
How can businesses reduce waiting times for customers?

Technology can help a lot. For example, banks and clinics can let people book appointments online, so they don't have to turn up and wait. Restaurants can use apps for ordering and paying. But if waiting can't be avoided, businesses should at least keep customers informed about how long it'll take, because uncertainty is often more frustrating than the wait itself.

p2.card: Describe a street market you have visited.
bullets: what you saw and bought there
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the market.
p2.sample:
The street market I'd like to describe is a night market in Chiang Mai, in the north of Thailand, which I visited with my sister about eighteen months ago during a short holiday.

It takes place every Sunday evening, when a long street in the old town is closed to traffic, and hundreds of stalls are set up along both sides. We went there on our second night, at around seven o'clock, just as it was getting dark, and by then it was already absolutely packed with both locals and tourists.

What struck me first was the variety of things on sale. There were handmade items like woven bags, silver jewellery and wooden carvings, as well as clothes and paintings by local artists. In the side streets and temple courtyards, there were food stalls selling everything from grilled sausages to mango sticky rice and fresh coconut ice cream. We also saw street performers, including a group of children playing traditional instruments, which was really charming.

In the end, I bought a hand-painted paper umbrella for my mother and a cotton shirt for myself, and I spent far too much on snacks. The prices were reasonable, but I tried a bit of bargaining, which the sellers seemed to expect.

Overall, I absolutely loved it. Even though it was crowded and very hot, the atmosphere was relaxed and friendly, and it felt like a genuine part of local life rather than something just for tourists. It also reminded me of the markets in my own country, but with a slightly calmer, more artistic feel.
vocab: nghệ sĩ biểu diễn đường phố
a genuine part of local life
một phần thực sự của đời sống địa phương
p3: Why do tourists like visiting local markets?
Do you think traditional markets will be replaced by supermarkets?
What are the advantages of buying food from small sellers?
Should street vendors be allowed to sell on the pavement?
How has online shopping affected small businesses?
p3samples: Do you think traditional markets will be replaced by supermarkets?

Not completely, at least not in the near future. Supermarkets are growing fast in Vietnamese cities because they're clean, air-conditioned and have fixed prices. But many people, especially older shoppers, still prefer traditional markets because the produce is fresher and they have personal relationships with the sellers. I think markets will survive, though they may need to modernise, for instance by improving hygiene and accepting digital payments.
Should street vendors be allowed to sell on the pavement?

It's a tricky balance. Street vendors are a big part of the culture and many families depend on them for their income. But when pavements are completely blocked, pedestrians are forced to walk in the road, which is dangerous. So I'd suggest licensing vendors and allowing them in specific areas or at certain times, rather than either banning them entirely or letting them occupy every space.

p2.card: Describe a person you know who has an interesting job.
p2.explain: and explain why you think their job is interesting.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about my cousin Lan, who works as a wildlife vet at a rescue centre for endangered animals in a national park. She's about five years older than me, and whenever our family gets together, everyone wants to hear her latest stories.

Her job involves looking after animals that have been injured or rescued from illegal trading, such as pangolins, monkeys and sometimes even bears. She examines them when they arrive, treats their injuries, and then monitors their recovery. The ultimate goal is to release as many as possible back into the wild, although some animals are too badly hurt and have to stay at the centre permanently.

She didn't follow a direct path into it. After graduating in veterinary science, she worked at an ordinary pet clinic in the city for a couple of years, treating cats and dogs. But she always felt she wanted to do something with a bigger impact, so she started volunteering at the rescue centre at weekends. When a full-time position came up, they offered it to her because she'd already proved how committed she was.

I find her job fascinating for several reasons. Firstly, every day is completely different, and she often has to work out how to treat species that very few vets have experience with. Secondly, it's genuinely meaningful work, because she's helping to protect animals that might otherwise disappear. Of course, it's not glamorous. She works long hours in hot, muddy conditions, and it can be heartbreaking when an animal doesn't survive. But she says she can't imagine doing anything else.
vocab: động vật có nguy cơ tuyệt chủng
có một vị trí tuyển dụng
p3: What jobs are considered most desirable in your country?
Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?
Why do some people change careers later in life?
Should young people follow their passion when choosing a job?
Which jobs do you think will disappear in the future?
p3samples: Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?

Ideally you'd have both, but if I had to choose, I'd lean towards an interesting job, as long as the salary covers your basic needs. You spend a huge portion of your life at work, and if you're bored every day, the money won't really compensate for that. That said, for people supporting a family or paying off debts, a good salary is understandably the priority, so it depends on your circumstances.
Which jobs do you think will disappear in the future?

Jobs that involve repetitive tasks are probably most at risk, things like cashiers, data entry clerks and some factory roles, because machines and artificial intelligence can do them faster and more cheaply. Even parts of jobs like translation or customer service are being automated. However, roles that require empathy, creativity or physical skill in unpredictable environments, such as nursing or plumbing, should be much harder to replace.

p2.card: Describe a time when you tried a food for the first time.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about it.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe the first time I tried durian, which, if you don't know, is a large, spiky tropical fruit that is famous for its incredibly strong smell. Some people say it smells like old socks, and it's actually banned on public transport and in many hotels in parts of Southeast Asia.

It might sound strange, since I'm Vietnamese and durian is very common here, but I'd always avoided it because of the smell. Then, about four years ago, I went on a trip to the Mekong Delta with some colleagues, and we visited a fruit orchard where the owner offered us durian that had just been picked. Everyone else in the group loved it, and they kept teasing me, saying I couldn't call myself a real southerner until I'd tried it.

So finally I gave in. The owner cut it open with a big knife, and inside there were these soft, pale yellow sections. I held my breath and took a small bite. Honestly, the texture surprised me most. It was creamy, almost like custard, and the taste was sweet with a slightly bitter, nutty flavour that's quite hard to describe.

As for how I felt, I'd say my reaction was mixed. I was proud of myself for being brave, and I could understand why people are so passionate about it. But I still couldn't get past the smell, which seemed to stay on my hands for hours. These days I'll eat a little bit if it's offered, especially in durian cakes, but I wouldn't say I'm a big fan.
vocab: kết cấu, độ mềm/cứng của món ăn
vượt qua, chấp nhận được điều gì
p3: Why are some people unwilling to try new foods?
How has the diet of people in your country changed in recent years?
Is it important for children to try a wide variety of foods?
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?
Should schools teach students how to cook?
p3samples: How has the diet of people in your country changed in recent years?

Quite dramatically, especially in the cities. People used to eat mainly rice, vegetables and fish cooked at home, but now fast food, sugary drinks and imported snacks are much more common. Food delivery apps have also made it easy to eat out every day. On the positive side, there's growing interest in healthy eating, so you see more salad bars, gyms and people checking nutrition labels.
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?

Absolutely. Food is often the first thing people associate with a country. Think of pho for Vietnam or pasta for Italy. Traditional dishes also carry history, because they show what ingredients were available, which foreign influences arrived and how people celebrated. When people move abroad, cooking food from home is one of the main ways they keep their culture alive, so it's far more than just something to eat.

p2.card: Describe a photo you took that you are proud of.
bullets: when and where you took it
p2.explain: and explain why you are proud of this photo.
p2.sample:
The photo I'm proudest of is one I took of my grandfather on the morning of his eightieth birthday. It shows him sitting on the wooden bench outside his house in the countryside, holding a cup of tea and laughing at something my little nephew had just said. The early sunlight is coming in from the side, so half of his face is lit up and you can see all the lines around his eyes.

I took it about two years ago. The whole family had gathered at his house for the celebration, and while everyone else was busy preparing food, I noticed him sitting outside on his own, looking really content.

I didn't have a professional camera, just my phone, but I'd been watching a lot of photography tutorials, so I tried to apply what I'd learned. I crouched down so that the camera was at his eye level, switched to portrait mode to blur the background, and turned off the flash so the light would look natural. I took around twenty shots, and this was the only one where he was laughing naturally rather than posing.

The reason I'm so proud of it is partly technical, because I think it's the first time I really got the light right. But mainly it's because it captures his personality perfectly, warm and full of humour. My family loved it so much that we had it printed and framed, and it now hangs in his living room. Sadly, his health has declined since then, so that photo has become even more precious to all of us.
vocab: lột tả được tính cách của ai
p3: Why do people take so many photos nowadays?
Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?
Is photography a real art form?
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?
How do you think people will store their memories in the future?
p3samples: Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?

Not really. Most people only post the highlights, like holidays, parties or special meals, and many photos are carefully edited or filtered. So what you see is a very selective version of someone's life. The risk is that viewers, especially teenagers, compare their own ordinary days with these perfect images and end up feeling inadequate, even though nobody's life actually looks like that all the time.
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?

Legally, in many countries, it's allowed, and I understand why, since street photography can record history and everyday life. But I think there's an ethical side too. If someone is clearly the main subject of the photo, it's polite to ask permission, especially before posting it online. And photographing children or people in vulnerable situations, like at a hospital, should definitely be avoided without consent.

p2.card: Describe a time when you received good news.
bullets: when and how you received it
p2.explain: and explain how you felt when you received the news.
p2.sample:
I'd like to describe the day I found out that I'd been awarded a scholarship for a short summer programme abroad. It was a six-week course in environmental management at a university in Australia, fully funded, including flights and accommodation.

I received the news about three years ago, in the middle of a very ordinary Tuesday. I was on my lunch break at work, scrolling through my emails, when I saw a message from the scholarship committee. I'd applied about four months earlier and had almost given up hope, because I'd heard that thousands of people applied for only a handful of places. So when I opened it, I had to read the first line three times before I really believed it said "Congratulations".

The first person I called was my mother. She was so excited that she started crying on the phone, and then she immediately rang all the relatives, so within an hour my whole extended family knew. That evening, my closest friends took me out for a celebratory dinner at a little hotpot restaurant we love.

As for how I felt, it was a mixture of emotions. Obviously I was thrilled and incredibly relieved, because I'd put a lot of effort into my application, writing and rewriting my personal statement many times. But I also felt a bit nervous, since I'd never travelled so far on my own before. Looking back, though, that experience was a real turning point. It gave me much more confidence and it's the main reason I later decided to continue studying in that field.

p3samples: Why do the media focus more on bad news than good news?

Partly it's human nature. We're naturally more alert to threats, so stories about disasters, crime or conflict grab our attention more than positive ones. And because media companies depend on clicks and viewing figures, they give audiences what keeps them watching. There's also a sense that bad news is more urgent, since it may require action, whereas good news often seems less important, even when it isn't.
Is it better to hear bad news in person or by message?

For serious news, like a death or a health problem, I think it should definitely be delivered in person or at least by phone. Hearing it from someone who can comfort you makes a big difference, and a text can feel cold or be misunderstood. However, for minor disappointments, like a cancelled event, a message is fine and even preferable, because it gives the person time to react privately.
